Abstract 
Recently, the brain-inspired mechanisms beneficial to efficient navigation in mammals have exhibited huge research 
potential. Specifically, the geometry cell model has shown significant insights into the ability of mammals, which 
is used to model the geometric information of their surroundings during movement. Meanwhile, the process 
of general exploration will consume large amounts of computing resources when agents with high-performance 
computing equipment accomplish autonomous tasks. This paper focuses on the long-range autonomous explora-
tion and navigation tasks in which they are conducted by agents within complex indoor and outdoor environments. 
To reduce the computational demands, we propose a framework integrating the Brain-Inspired Geometry-aware-
ness namely BIG for two autonomous tasks. The exploration task named BIG-Explorer involves efficiently searching 
untouched areas by embedding the geometry cell model. It identifies expanding frontiers using geometric assign-
ers and takes into account relevant factors such as boundary information. The navigation task named BIG-Navigator 
builds upon insights gained during the exploration phase and guides agents to a predefined destination. We con-
duct comprehensive experimental assessments within third-party simulation environments. The evaluation metrics 
employed in this paper include the number of nodes, the length of a path, algorithm execution time, and the size 
of exploration space. Finally, the results of the evaluation demonstrate that the incorporation of geometry cell model 
increases the efficiency in both exploration and navigation processes by at least 20% , compared with four benchmark 
methods.

Introduction
In the cognitive neuroscience research, the autonomous 
navigation of intelligent agents constitutes a significant 
objective, which embodies machine intelligence like a 
human being. A critical challenge lies in integrating theo-
retical foundations from brain-inspired research with 
exploring unknown space and navigating to a destination 
in various scenarios. Although many algorithms based 
on optimization and heuristics have been intensively 
studied, the brain-inspired navigation primarily focuses 
on scenarios of autonomous exploration. These complex 
scenarios are narrow, multi-structured, and similarly 
characterized where agents explore the space stocking in 
the local optimum and excessive number of nodes. Thus 
different scenarios are crucial for evaluating the suc-
cess rate and resource consumption of navigation tasks. 
Assessment metrics are used for statistics including time 
consumption and the explored space in the process of 
reaching a predefined target.
The brain is characterized by its unstructured yet effi-
cient approach to complex scenes because of its adept 
organizational structure. This characterization could be

Much biological navigation research has been conducted 
in the past eight decades. In 1948, the cognitive map was 
discussed as a concept of environmental description in 
Tolman’s seminal work (Tolman, 1948). More specifically, 
experience maps are studied as a basic form of cognitive 
maps. Studies have shown that the storage and process-
ing of spatial information are associated with the hip-
pocampus (Ormond and O’Keefe, 2022). The place cell in 
the hippocampus plays a foundational role when a mam-
mal executes navigation tasks and builds the cognitive 
map. Similar cell models of perception help mammals 
to perceive surroundings, self-localize, and make policy 
decisions. In recent years, the geometry cell (Zeng et al., 
2022) offers a more precise representation of spatial geo-
metric information.
To that end, our paper proposes a novel framework 
named BIG that combines the mammalian geometry 
cell model with representative exploration and naviga-
tion tasks. This framework improves the efficiency of 
the agent exploration which determines optimal routes 
toward specified targets. Namely, this framework draws 
inspiration from the experience mapping structure that 
is built during the locomotion of both mammals and 
human beings. During a typical autonomous exploration 
shown in Fig. 1, a brain-inspired agent employs a suite of 
sensors, including camera and Lidar, for the perception 
of its surroundings.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 
1.	 Geometry cell models with geometry-awareness 
properties are applied for the first time in exploration 
and navigation tasks in long-range, unknown, and 
complex environments. Real-time boundary percep-
tion based on the brain-inspired model is integrated 
with a sampling-optimized stochastic search tree 
expansion algorithm to generate spatio-temporally 
adaptive sampling frontiers. This approach enables 
more comprehensive and faster exploration using 
fewer nodes.
2.	 This paper proposes a Brain-Inspired Geometry-
awareness (BIG) framework for exploration and 
navigation tasks. The BIG framework employs head 
direction cell and geometry cell models to achieve 
faster boundary-based coverage (BIG-Explorer) and 
vector-based self-supervised navigation of unknown 
environments (BIG-Navigator). The generated BIG-
Map, utilizing spatio-temporal clustering methods, 
consumes less storage space.
3.	 Sufficient experiments were conducted in various 
long-range scenarios. Compared to four state-of-
the-art methods, the proposed method can complete 
exploration and navigation tasks using fewer nodes, 
shorter path lengths, and higher algorithm efficiency 
in unknown environments such as campuses, forests, 
and indoor corridors.
The structure of this paper is as follows: Sect. “Related 
work” introduces the previous related work related to our 
research. Sects. “Methodology” and “Experiments and 
analysis” describe the core framework and experimental 
results respectively. Finally, the conclusion and future 
work in Sect. “Conclusion” are discussed briefly.

model within the hippocampus.

Autonomous exploration of space
It is an important topic for agents that know how to 
explore an unknown space efficiently and thoroughly, as 
highlighted by Thrun (2002). Durrant and Bailey (2006) 
and Lluvia et al. (2021) delivered comprehensive insights 
into robotic space exploration, covering exploration strat-
egies, perception techniques, and path planning meth-
ods. El-Sheimy and Li (2021) described the key problems 
in indoor navigation. Zhao et  al. (2023) discussed the 
current state of the art with brain-like mechanisms to 
combine navigation tasks.
The Rapid-exploration Random Tree (RRT), initially 
proposed by LaValle (1998), is a prominent method 
employed in the exploration process to sample expanded 
viewpoints from the horizon in each step. This explo-
ration process automatically collects comprehensive 
environmental data, encompassing obstacle identifica-
tion (Xu et al., 2022), and records of explored areas. The 
sensor data acquisition is used for the input of agent’s 
cognitive mechanism, enabling precise cognition of its 
surroundings. Yu et  al. (2023) proposes efficient brain-
like hardware platform architectures that can per-
form recognition of the surrounding environment. The 
acquired data includes detailed spatial information, 
establishing a foundational framework for informed deci-
sion-making in autonomous navigation. Brain-inspired 
place recognition algorithms for different scales are dis-
cussed in Wen et al. (2022).
The OctoMap (Hornung et al., 2013) functions as the 
foundational occupancy map, facilitating collision checks 
for viewpoints and the edges connecting them to ensure 
their placement in free space. Full information is needed 
to complete the overall exploration including velocity, 
rotation, and translation constraints described in Hua 
et al. (2023). These responses are likely shaped by sensory 
inputs from various modalities, including visual, audi-
tory, and vestibular cues (Graham et al., 2023). The mag-
nitude and density of events should be considered in Gu 
et al. (2022). Jiang et al. (2022), Li et al. (2023), and Zhang 
et al. (2022) proposed the relocalization methods of the 
agent.
Notably, researchers attempt to explain the above 
exploration process from a neuroscience perspective. 
Geometry cells in convex mazes or simulated environ-
ments display consistent firing patterns, reflecting spe-
cific geometric segments. Significant changes occur at 
compartment junctions, signaling abrupt shifts in local 
spatial geometry. These changes could potentially sup-
port the topological representation and target identifica-
tion of environments composed of multiple sub-regions 
of different shapes.
brain‑inspired navigation within long‑range scenes
To date, a significant focus is on various research endeav-
ors in the field of class brain navigation, particularly 
directed towards tasks such as passive map construction, 
path planning, and policy learning. These efforts are pri-
marily motivated by task-specific goals or specific target 
points. Some studies have delved into the complexities of 
active Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM), 
with particular emphasis on controlling the camera 
actively for map generation. In addressing these chal-
lenges, most methodologies adopt an approach based on 
Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POM-
DPs) (Spaan, 2012). These methods aim to approximate 
or minimize map uncertainty as a means of solving the 
underlying problems.
Another class of autonomous navigation methods 
involves selecting vantage points, often situated on fron-
tiers between explored and unexplored regions. Recent 
works expanded by Chen et  al. (2019) and Fang et  al. 
(2019) solve this problem with learning-based methodol-
ogies. Some exploration policies combine the above two 
types of methods. Many results show the improvements 
over the individual methods.
A lot of investigations in autonomous exploration con-
centrates on integrating Reinforcement Learning (RL) 
to imitate the decision-making learning mechanism of 
the brain, including Mirowski et al. (2018) and Li et al. 
(2019). A deep reinforcement learning model is applied 
to goal-driven visual navigation in simulation environ-
ments (Zhu et al., 2017) based on research in (Mnih et al., 
2015). In various tasks, agents are initialized at several 
random locations within mazes or other environments 
(Banino et  al., 2018). These agents are set to reach the 
same goal in comparative experiments.

An innovative progress with the biologically inspired 
idea is proposing a bionic polarized light perception 
method. It extracts directional information from pat-
terns, offering the distinct advantages of robust anti-
interference capabilities and the absence of cumulative 
error (Wang et al., 2016).
Concurrently, Milford introduced RatSLAM (Milford 
et  al., 2016), a system inspired by the working princi-
ples of the hippocampus, and designed for positional 
acquisition and mapping. RatSLAM introduces a novel 
cell model termed the pose cell which mirrors the Con-
tinuous Attractor Network (CAN) structure of the 
brain(Burak and Fiete, 2009). The CAN integrates the 
visual landmark information from cameras and the agent 
itself. Notably, the odometer information of an agent is 
updated during navigation. In 1980, Mittelstaedt and 
Mittelstaedt (1982) first introduced the concept of path 
integration. In contrast to traditional SLAM algorithms, 
RatSLAM mimics the brain’s neural network structure, 
constructs a grid topology, and relies on landmarks for 
localization. This concept is closely related to the Dead 
Reckoning (DR) method, which provides a means of cal-
culating the current position based on previously known 
positions(Edelkamp and Schrödl, 2012). The attention 
mechanism in neural networks is first combined with 
SLAM in Li et al. (2020).
This spatial representation forms the cognitive 
map(Whittington et al., 2022). The cognitive map under 
the Cartesian coordinate system can reflect the relative 
position between nodes, but lacks cognitive ability and 
is difficult to describe the logical and hierarchical rela-
tionships between nodes. The representation model of a 
cognitive map (Whittington et al., 2022) breaks through 
the constraints of the classic Cartesian coordinate system 
(Redish and Touretzky, 1997) that this map offers flexibil-
ity in the agent’s location. Experimental results indicate 
the algorithm’s ability to achieve more robust positioning 
and mapping in larger spatial environments.
Although much progress has been made in the field 
of brain-inspired navigation and path planning, several 
challenges remain in research on exploration and naviga-
tion tasks in long-range environments.
First, current brain-inspired navigation and plan-
ning capabilities are insufficient for the tasks in long-
range, unknown, and complex environments. Presently, 
brain-inspired positioning and recognition primarily 
operate in long-range scenes, requiring the intelligent 
agent has the prior knowledge of the environment. Addi-
tionally, brain-inspired models are typically validated in 
small-scale settings, which leads to more uncertainty and 
less robustness when scaled up.
Secondly, existing methods are not fully based on bio-
logical principles for understanding space and perform-
ing navigation tasks. Detailed spatial representation 
requires accurate and dense scene nodes, needing sig-
nificant computational resources and large storage space, 
which contradicts the efficiency observed in biological 
systems.
Finally, brain-inspired navigation models rely on the 
cooperation of multiple cell types for perception, cog-
nition, and navigation. However, current approaches 
mainly use grid cell theory for positioning and recogni-
tion tasks, with insufficient incorporation of biological 
mechanisms in exploration tasks.
The BIG represents the first attempt to incorporate 
brain-inspired algorithms into exploration tasks. Specifi-
cally, the BIG leverages geometry-awareness to achieve 
efficient exploration of unknown environments. The 
method in this article can perform exploration tasks in 
completely unfamiliar environments and scale up the 
environment from tens of meters to hundreds of meters. 
After completing the exploration with the help of geom-
etry-awareness capabilities, the space passed by the intel-
ligent agent can almost cover the entire environment, 
helping to smoothly execute the next navigation task.
Methodology
The architecture of BIG
The architecture of BIG of in this paper consists of four 
modules including the geometric information, BIG-
Explorer, BIG-Navigator, and BIG-Map as shown in 
Fig. 2.
The four modules drive agents to finish tasks of 
autonomous exploration and navigation. The geometry 
cell model participates in the exploration process of an 
agent by mirroring the navigation mechanism of mam-
mals. The agent leverages biological features to explore 
the environments as fast as possible, which is proposed 
as the Faster-Expanding algorithm. The agent explores 
its surroundings to sense the structure of the environ-
ment and ultimately form experience maps used for tar-
get-navigation. The process of constructing experience 
maps requires the optimization assigner module. Navi-
gating towards the target could help the agent find the 
destination. A predefined destination serves as a guiding 
parameter that directs the autonomous agent with preci-
sion and efficiency in completing the full path-searching 
process.

The geometry cell model is one kind of EBC in a broad 
sense that this model takes its HD as the spatial refer-
ence. Geometry cells, EBCs, and grid cells reflect an 
organism’s perceptual encoding of motion, position, and 
space, forming egocentric representations of local or 
global environments. However, significant differences 
exist between geometry cells and grid cells. First, their 
anatomical locations differ: grid cells are found in the 
entorhinal cortex, while geometry cells are situated in the 
posterior olfactory cortex. Second, they process different 
types of information. Grid cells primarily encode posi-
tional and motion data, whereas geometry cells focus on 
the geometric properties of local space, particularly the 
distance and direction relative to boundary viewpoints. 
In terms of encoding mechanisms, grid cells employ a 
hexagonal grid to encode positional information, while 
geometry cells use a product of Gaussian and von Mises 
functions. Lastly, grid cells capture multiple spatial posi-
tions experienced during navigation, while geometry cells 
encode the geometric characteristics of local space and 
assist in constructing spatial cognitive maps.

Abstract: Recently, the brain-inspired mechanisms beneficial to efficient navigation in mammals have exhibited huge research potential. Specifically, the geometry cell model has shown significant insights into the ability of mammals, which is used to model the geometric information of their surroundings during movement. Meanwhile, the process of general exploration will consume large amounts of computing resources when agents with high-performance computing equipment accomplish autonomous tasks. This paper focuses on the long-range autonomous explora- tion and navigation tasks in which they are conducted by agents within complex indoor and outdoor environments. To reduce the computational demands, we propose a framework integrating the Brain-Inspired Geometry-aware- ness namely BIG for two autonomous tasks. The exploration task named BIG-Explorer involves efficiently searching untouched areas by embedding the geometry cell model. It identifies expanding frontiers using geometric assign- ers and takes into account relevant factors such as boundary information. The navigation task named BIG-Navigator builds upon insights gained during the exploration phase and guides agents to a predefined destination. We con- duct comprehensive experimental assessments within third-party simulation environments. The evaluation metrics employed in this paper include the number of nodes, the length of a path, algorithm execution time, and the size of exploration space. Finally, the results of the evaluation demonstrate that the incorporation of geometry cell model increases the efficiency in both exploration and navigation processes by at least 20% , compared with four benchmark methods.
